articles.title_orig: David Ellison Taps Mattel’s Ynon Kreiz to Be Co-CEO of Merged Paramount-Warner Bros.
articles.title_zh: David Ellison Taps Mattel’s Ynon Kreiz to Be Co-CEO of Merged Paramount-Warner Bros.
articles.content_orig:
Ynon Kreiz , who is stepping down as CEO of Mattel after eight years , will join David Ellison ’s Paramount — which is expected to close its mega-merger with Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6 — as co-CEO of the new company, Paramount announced.
As chairman and CEO, Ellison will lead all strategy, creative and technology functions. Kreiz, as co-CEO, will oversee the company’s day-to-day operations and integration of the combined businesses. It’s a “pairing that joins complementary skillsets to amplify results,” Paramount said in announcing the appointment Wednesday. The businesses of the combined company (whose name has not yet been announced) will report jointly to both Ellison and Kreiz.
Kreiz will start at Paramount on Oct. 5, 2026, as co-CEO. He also will join the company’s board of directors.
News of Kreiz’s hiring came shortly after Paramount cleared the final step before it could close the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger when a judge approved the company’s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by 12 state attorneys general. The merger is expected to close Oct. 6, according to Paramount regulatory filings.
Ellison’s appointment of Kreiz “caps a long-term plan: pursue both Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, then partner with a leading executive of his caliber to integrate, operationalize and manage the businesses as they build one of the most ambitious next-generation media companies in the industry’s history,” according to Paramount’s announcement.
One source close to the situation told Variety said that Ellison’s courting of Kreiz has been in the works for months and was “another ace up Ellison’s sleeve.”
Ellison, in a companywide memo Wednesday about Kreiz’s appointment, wrote, “We still have work to do before the [Warner Bros.] deal closes, and nothing changes until it does. But I wanted you to hear this from me first. I hope you’re as excited as I am to welcome Ynon to our leadership team.”
Ellison said in a statement: “Bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery to create a next-generation global media company is a transformational moment for our industry. Leading it takes a rare combination of strategic vision, operational depth and experience running a public company at the highest levels of media. Ynon brings all three. In Ynon, I’m adding a partner with strong leadership and the operating firepower this integration demands. It’s a division of labor built on our complementary strengths, with clear reporting lines and it lets me focus where I can contribute most: long-term strategy, the company’s overall creative direction, talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation. We’re like-minded, we see this business the same way and there’s no one I’d rather partner with. Together we’ll build one integrated company that is creator-first, tech-forward and built to scale globally.”
Kreiz said in a statement provided by Paramount: “I’m excited to partner with David to build the next-generation media and entertainment company — bringing together premium content and iconic brands at the highest quality and scale, serving global audiences across every entertainment vertical and distribution platform. David is a unique talent and executive: a rare blend of business acumen, creative instinct, and clear vision. I very much share that vision, and I’m inspired by what we can accomplish together. The industry is at an inflection point, demanding evolution, investment, and a willingness to rethink business models. I look forward to working with the leadership team to build a cohesive global entertainment platform — one that stands out with best-in-class operations and execution powered by technology, with unparalleled creative relationships, production capabilities, and global reach. We will continue empowering creators, make this company a greenfield for innovation and storytelling, and collaborate with key partners to reach and engage fans worldwide.”
Gerry Cardinale, founder and managing partner of RedBird Capital Partners — Paramount’s co-controlling shareholder and a member of its board of directors — praised Ellison’s ability to lead the company through two “historic acquisitions.” In August 2025, Skydance Media closed the deal to acquire Paramount Global. Cardinale added that Ellison has at the same time been “running the business and building a team that’s already exceeding our synergy targets, beating our financial metrics, and never wavering on our commitment to the creative community.”
Mattel earlier Wednesday announced that Kreiz will step down as chairman and CEO effective Oct. 2, “to take a senior leadership position at another public company.” Roger Lynch, Condé Nast’s CEO, has been named Mattel’s next CEO.
Kreiz, a veteran media exec, is the former chairman and CEO of Maker Studios, a YouTube-oriented digital content network acquired by Disney in 2014. Kreiz exited Disney in 2016 and joined Mattel in 2018 . From 2008-11, he served as chairman and CEO of Endemol Group, and before that was a general partner at venture-capital firm Balderton Capital (formerly Benchmark Capital Europe) from 2005-07. Earlier in his career, Kreiz co-founded and was chairman and CEO of Fox Kids Europe.
Mattel has credited Kreiz with boosting its market share across key toy categories, ranking No. 1 globally in dolls, vehicles, and infant, toddler and preschool segments. Mattel also noted that Kreiz oversaw Mattel Studios’ first theatrical release, “Barbie” starring Margot Robbie, which was the top global box office film of 2023 and has stood as Warner Bros. Pictures’ highest-grossing movie of all time.
Said Cardinale, “Ynon has spent his career at the intersection of media, technology and franchise-building — pairing extraordinary storytelling with the technology to deliver it to fans everywhere. He understands not just how fans connect with the IP they love, but the economics that make entertainment endure. Great leaders accomplish great things. Historic ones know when to bring in the right partner to make it last — and that’s what David has done. It’s exactly why the company will have the operational firepower and the cutting-edge leadership to win.”
Along with Kreiz, the leadership of the combined Paramount-WBD is already taking shape. Casey Bloys, head of WBD’s HBO, is poised to assume oversight of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. streaming business after Cindy Holland announced Tuesday she was stepping down from her role running Paramount+ and other direct-to-consumer.

articles.content_orig:
The Lady Greyhounds may have defeated Bristol City 4-2 during the penultimate Season 4 episode of "Ted Lasso," but the team still suffered a tremendous loss: Mae Green, one of their staunchest supporters — played since Season 1 by Annette Badland — died in the stands shortly after watching them pull off a miraculous comeback .
"It's devastating," Tanya Reynolds, who plays Alice, tells TVLine. Abbie Hern, who plays Gemma, calls Mae's death "absolutely heartbreaking," particularly after the pub owner revealed that she'd once dreamed of becoming a professional footballer herself, at a time when women weren't afforded that opportunity. "I think the team will be absolutely devastated — but, in a way, also so thankful that the game ended the way that it did, and they got to give her those moments," Hern says — including riding on the bus with the ladies and joining them in the locker room ahead of the match.
Mae's words about the path that wasn't available to her carry particular resonance for Alice and Gemma, whose complicated relationships with football — and with each other — have come into sharper focus.
After Gemma was injured in Episode 8 , Alice explained to Rebecca how quickly an injured player can go from being surrounded by concerned teammates to watching everyone move on without them, strongly suggesting that she'd experienced that isolation herself when her own playing career abruptly ended. Alice also opened up to Gemma about how much she still misses playing, while a visit to Gemma's home shed new light on why the footballer had struggled to choose between law school and the sport she loves.
Their newfound understanding was put to the test in Episode 9, when Gemma took a scary fall but insisted on taking — and scored — a crucial penalty kick. When Alice subsequently told her she shouldn't return for the second half of the game, Gemma listened.
In the Q&A below, Reynolds and Hern unpack Alice's vulnerability and unresolved grief, Gemma's decision to commit to football, and the trust that's finally developed between the former teammates.
TVLINE | Alice is at her most vulnerable when Ted finds her having a panic attack in Episode 8. Rather than press her to explain what's wrong, he simply joins her in a series of deep breaths. What does it mean for Alice to have someone understand what she needs in that moment without her having to say it? REYNOLDS | Oh, it was huge. To be caught crying at work was probably her absolute worst nightmare. It was her in her most vulnerable state. It's probably the most exposed and the most honest that she's been, and [she was] thinking she's completely alone. And so for Ted to walk in was mortifying for her. But by that point, it's too late. She's there. Her skin has been peeled off.
And the best possible thing he could have done was just sit with her and not try to talk to her, because she wouldn't have wanted to. She does say, "I don't even know why I'm crying," and obviously she knows, but she doesn't want to lift the lid on it. She doesn't want to go into it. And so for him to just sit there next to her and be there for her, and with her , and not judging her at all , is the best thing that he could have done. And then to speak to her indirectly through the team meant a lot to her as well.
TVLINE | When Alice described to Rebecca what it's like to be injured and slowly watch everyone move on without you, it gave us such a clear sense of what losing football did to her. How much of Alice's wall — her anger, her defensiveness this season — came from grief over a career that she hasn't fully processed? REYNOLDS | Oh, God, so much! She's not really processed it at all. Being in that coaching position and being around all these players that have so much potential and have the opportunity that she now no longer has and would do anything for, she probably wasn't prepared for how much it would all hurt. Because she's not over it. She's not ready to not be a player anymore.
If she was comfortable and at ease with where she was in her life and with her new path as a coach, she'd be a much softer, warmer, easier person. But you can feel it. It's right beneath the surface — this grief that she's not living the life that she always thought she would be, and that she always wanted, and that she was so, so close to.
TVLINE | We got our first real glimpse into Gemma's home life in Episode 8. She comes from a wealthy family, her mother is eager for her to pursue a law internship, and her father was a footballer. How much did that context help you understand why Gemma had been torn between law school and football? HERN | It absolutely explains it. We had that conversation early on: "Well, why is she doing this? Why is she committing to two things that deserve 100% of her commitment?" Because she's not necessarily an indecisive person. She's just faced with a challenge that's a lot deeper than not being able to pick one thing.
It's really nice to have that and to be able to explore that in that episode. She joined the team because she missed football, she thought, but actually, the reasons are much more vast. And Alice knows that. [She] knows that it's much more than you just being good at it and wanting to do it because you're good at it. It really means something to her.
TVLINE | Gemma takes a scary fall in Episode 9 but still insists on taking that penalty kick herself. Is she facing her fears, ignoring what her body is telling her, or simply determined to prove that she can keep going? HERN | She has spent the whole episode convincing the coaches that she's good. She's good, she's great, and she's able to come back on. And so taking the penalty was like, "I told you I could score a goal. I'm ready. I told you." That's that part of Gemma's drive and her motivation to prove to everyone what she's made of. And even after the twinge, if Alice didn't say to her, "Are you OK?" and make her really admit it, she probably would have carried on even further. She's got a lot to prove.
TVLINE | When Alice tells Gemma at halftime that she shouldn't play the second half, Gemma accepts it without putting up a fight. Why is she willing to listen to Alice in that moment, after pushing back against her for so much of the season? REYNOLDS | Because, just in the last two episodes — if you think about all the stuff that happens in Episode 8 — Alice really redeems herself in Gemma's eyes. The last time you see them in Episode 8, they're at the hospital, and Alice has been really vulnerable with Gemma in a way that she hasn't been before. She's opened up with that whole speech about how she misses playing football so much and why she's so envious of Gemma and her f–king knees. And so they've softened quite immensely, because by the time they're in the hospital, Alice goes with her to her MRI. You don't see it, but you see us leaving together when you're in the wheelchair. She's with her, and her own mother isn't there. Alice has worked really hard to earn a place of trust in Gemma's eyes. HERN | I completely agree. She's not just there for her when she's playing well. She's there regardless. REYNOLDS | And she's also demonstrating that she's in it for the long game with Gemma. She's like, "Don't f–king play this half, because we're in it for the long haul, and I'm going to be here for the long haul as long as you are." It just shows that she has faith in her entire career, which probably means a lot to her.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf rejected claims by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Iran faces an imminent economic collapse, arguing instead that Washington is heading toward a debt crisis of its own.
Responding on X to Bessent’s assertion earlier Wednesday that Tehran could have “nothing left to trade” within two weeks, Ghalibaf used memes to point to what he saw as U.S. economic vulnerabilities.
Among them was a mock financial model titled “Trajectory of Stress on the House,” which contended that ballooning national debt, rising Treasury bond yields and energy costs will place mounting strain on the American financial system.
Ghalibaf also paired the mock formula with a cartoon depicting Bessent as Wile E. Coyote running off a cliff.
Jonathan Ernst / POOL / AFP via Getty Images
Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered the Iranian delegation attending the United Nations General Assembly to immediately leave the United States, officials said Wednesday.
“Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome,” an official told Fox News Digital.
“The United Nations General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go,” they added.
The Iranian diplomatic delegation had arrived in New York on Sept. 22 to attend the annual summit and met with a U.S. team for talks on the sidelines.
Hormuz / AP Photo / Vahid Salemi
Oil prices rose Wednesday, with Brent crude posting its biggest monthly gain since July, as stalled U.S.-Iran peace talks and tightening U.S. fuel markets fueled concerns about global supply, Reuters reported.
Brent crude for November delivery, which expires Wednesday, settled up 91 cents, or 0.9%, at $103.50 a barrel. The December contract rose $1.87, or 1.9%, to $98.03 a barrel.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude settled up $1.04, or 1.2%, at $90.42 a barrel.
For September, Brent gained about 14% which was its strongest monthly performance since July. WTI advanced roughly 5%, Reuters reported.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on Wednesday defended U.S. military action against Tehran as necessary while speaking at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit .
Rutte argued that only Washington had the capability to neutralize Tehran’s nuclear capacity and the threat he warned extends “not only for Israel and the Middle East ” but to Europe as well.
While agreeing that the war carries clear “downsides,” the Rutte urged European allies to increase defense investments so they can eventually “take care of their backyard themselves” and secure key waterways like the Red Sea from the Houthis rather than relying on the U.S.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said Wednesday that U.S. forces destroyed major elements of Iran’s military and crippled its nuclear ambitions during operations against Tehran.
“Take Iran, for example. Allow me to lay it out simply,” Hegseth said at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia.
“For the anti-American losers in our media. These Americans right here and their peers, these have destroyed Iran's Navy, destroyed Iran's Air Force, destroyed their air defense systems, their leadership and their military-industrial capacity, their entire defense base.”
Hegseth said Iran’s “conventional shield has been crippled” and its nuclear ambitions have been “laid bare for the world.”
“This group is ensuring that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon. Courageous and historic operations that every red-blooded American is proud of,” he added
U.S. Central Command announced plans for its first multinational attack drone task force on Wednesday, bringing together what it said were U.S. and regional forces to operate unmanned systems across air and sea.
"We're excited to welcome Bahrain to Task Force Falcon Strike after the kingdom affirmed its commitment to join CENTCOM in building the world's first multinational attack drone unit,” the command said on X .
“Bahrain is a steadfast partner in strengthening regional security and stability,” Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM commander, said.
“The United States military has a lot of strong partnerships and friends in the region,” Cooper said, referring to the Middle East.
“We are collectively stronger when we integrate and deploy new capabilities together,” he said in a statement.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi flatly rejected U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s assertion Wednesday that there were indications Tehran was involved in the suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford.
“PM Burnham says the U.K. government ‘can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part’ in the RAF Fairford incident,” Araghchi said in a post on X .
“I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all.
“You’re barking up the wrong tree,” he added.
Earlier Wednesday, Burnham said there were “strong indications” Iran played a role in a suspected plot near RAF Fairford, which has been a hub for U.S. bombers during military operations against Iran.
“But of course, it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America,” Burnham had also said in an interview with the BBC .
President Donald Trump on Wednesday said the U.S. will soon have to decide whether to "blow up" Iran or reach a deal with Tehran, warning the standoff is ending imminently.
“Maybe you blow them up,” he told reporters at the Oval Office. “We have to make that decision. We blow them up, make a deal.
“But the time is coming,” he warned. "It's going to end very soon, one way or the other.”
President Donald Trump said Wednesday the U.S. is "studying" whether Iran was involved in a suspected terror plot targeting RAF Fairford, a key U.S.-used air base in Britain, while questioning the U.K.'s handling of the case and promising answers "very quickly."
“We are. I look, we are studying it right now,” Trump said in the Oval Office.
“We're studying it. We're studying it very hard,” he assured.
“Iran's got a lot of problems right there. You know, they have no money. Their currency is dead. Their economy is dead. Their military is gone. They have no military. They have no navy. They have no air force. And their leaders are fighting for control," he said.
“I think their leaders are fighting very strongly for control. But control of what? So but we'll have an answer to that very quickly,” Trump added.
Asked whether he was satisfied with how the United Kingdom was handling the case, Trump pointed to the release of the five men and said authorities caught them “wanting to blow up a base.”
“We caught them early,” Trump said.
“Maybe they did it for a reason, but we're going to know about that this afternoon," Trump added.
President Donald Trump on Wednesday hailed the U.S. withdrawal from Iraq, marking the end of a military presence that began 23 years ago, and said American forces left with all of their equipment intact while pledging Washington would continue to assist Iraq if needed.
“We're now gone and we took everything with us, every, every nut, every bolt, every screw,” he told reporters in the Oval Office.
“Every tank, every plane,” he added.
“We should have left a long time ago,” Trump said before adding that the United States left with “dignity and respect.”
Trump also said that after the withdrawal, Washington would “be there to help if we need to.”
“But that's a big thing. We're out of Iraq after 23 years,” he said.
“If you look at Iraq, we lost 4,500 people. And the result isn't anywhere near what we have here, although we went into Iraq to destroy ISIS, and I did that in my first term.
“That's why they should have left. Long ago.
“But the sole reason we went to Iraq was to eradicate ISIS, and I did it in my first term.”

articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic's IPO pitch embraces AI's promise and peril
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic says its AI models could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity” and can “resist shutdown,” according to an initial public offering prospectus obtained by Reuters.
Anthropic is pursuing an IPO some time in the next year that many expect to value the five-year-old company at approximately $2 trillion. The company’s Wall Street debut will follow a June public offering by SpaceX, which owed much of its $2 trillion opening day valuation to its own AI efforts. OpenAI , the other leading American AI company, has announced plans for its own public offering.
The Anthropic IPO could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company. But the company behind Claude also warned in the prospectus that its AI models can have “self-preserving behaviors” and have attempted to “conceal or manipulate information” and engaged in behavior “resembling blackmail” according to the report.
Why AI companies are choosing to go public
The run of AI public offerings not only gives individual and institutional investors a chance to cash in on the AI boom, but also provides more transparency about their businesses. Yet the IPOs come amid growing concerns about AI’s advancement and capabilities.
An AI agent from OpenAI, Anthropic’s chief rival, broke into an Australian healthcare database, the country’s prime minister revealed last week. OpenAI also disclosed Friday that its agents probed three US government websites without authorization, but in that case did not obtain non-public data.
In a prospectus, companies typically offer investors lists of risks they face, such as lawsuits and competitive pressures, when laying out the case for investing in the company. But the hazards are never this stark. Anthropic dedicated 80 pages to its risk factors in the leaked prospectus, significantly more than the 48 pages it spent detailing its business, according to Reuters.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from CNN.
The prospectus is likely to feed growing concerns about the risks posed to humanity by AI. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon received widespread attention when he left the company and posted on X that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic is one of the leading companies in AI development, and its CEO Dario Amodei responded to Coxon’s post with a 3,800 word essay calling for a slowdown and guardrails on the development of AI. He also told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed. Amodei wrote in his essay that the risks are serious, even if the benefits could change humanity for the better.
Some in the industry, however, including the CEO of Hugging Face, which was breached by OpenAI’s AI models when they acted without authorization during a test, believe the fears are overblown.
President Donald Trump is set to meet with executives from the industry Tuesday, including Amodei, in a summit aimed at coming to a consensus in the industry. Trump has repeatedly resisted calls to regulate AI and has dismissed concerns as a “hoax.”
AI stocks slide after top industry CEOs call for slowdown of technology’s development
AI giants need to raise a great amount of money to fund their costly development plans, and the massive amount of AI spending among big tech companies on computing infrastructure and talent has sent jitters through Wall Street.
The leaked Anthropic IPO filing sheds light on its financials, revealing that the company lost $42 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. The company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure obligations in coming year, and said that nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from two customers.
Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in May.

On September 9, 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported that John Ternus took the stage for the first time as Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )'s chief executive. He became just the third CEO since Steve Jobs returned to the company in 1997 and used his debut product launch to introduce the foldable iPhone Duo alongside a strategic decision to eliminate baseline iPhone 18 models in favor of steering buyers toward Pro and Pro Max tiers.
Ternus, a 25-year Apple veteran who led hardware engineering since 2021 and personally oversaw development of the foldable iPhone, took over from Tim Cook on September 1 after 15 years of Cook's leadership.
Don't Miss: Cook Hands Ternus Apple (AAPL) that Still has to Prove itself on AI
John Ternus brings deep product-development experience to Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ) as he takes over the company. Ternus spent years running Apple's hardware engineering organization and oversaw development across the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and AirPods before becoming CEO. He now begins his tenure with Apple's first foldable iPhone and one of the company's biggest hardware redesigns in years. It gives investors a leader with direct experience managing the products that generate most of Apple's revenue.
Apple is using higher-end products and selective price increases to protect economics as memory and storage costs rise sharply. The company raised the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max starting prices by $100 to $1,199 and $1,299 after surging memory costs pressured the electronics industry. Apple also chose not to refresh its base iPhone and Air models at the event, concentrating its newest hardware on premium devices that can better absorb component inflation and support stronger revenue per device.
The first major launch under Ternus shows that Apple prepared a substantive product transition rather than simply changing leadership. Ternus used his first event as CEO to introduce the $1,999 iPhone Duo, upgraded Pro models, and an AI strategy built around on-device processing and privacy. Tim Cook also moved to executive chairman instead of leaving Apple entirely. It gives Ternus access to continuity at the top while he establishes his own product strategy and pushes Apple further into AI-enabled hardware.
Look Into: Apple (AAPL)'s New CEO Bets Big on a $1,999 Foldable iPhone
Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )'s premium-focused launch strategy could make demand more sensitive to price. The iPhone 18 Pro now starts at $1,199, the Pro Max at $1,299, and the foldable Duo at $1,999. Apple left the base iPhone and Air without new generations at this event. Existing lower-priced models remain available. But Apple must still convince consumers that the newest hardware justifies significantly higher prices as component inflation pushes smartphones further into premium territory.
Ternus inherits Apple at a moment when the company still needs to prove that its AI strategy can match its hardware strength. Apple enters his tenure while playing catch-up in artificial intelligence, even as Ternus now positions privacy and on-device processing as key differentiators. Apple's scale gives the company enormous resources. However, the new CEO must turn Siri AI and Apple Intelligence into compelling everyday products while competitors continue investing aggressively in generative AI.
Apple also faces real supply and margin pressure as Ternus starts his tenure. The firm reported a 48.1% gross margin excluding tariff benefits in fiscal Q3 as rising memory costs weighed on profitability. Management warned that significant supply constraints could restrict product availability. Apple can raise prices to offset some of those pressures, but higher prices could eventually weaken demand, forcing Ternus to balance margins, unit growth, and supply availability during his first major product cycle as CEO.
Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )'s hedge fund count was nearly flat at 169 funds in the second quarter versus 170 in the first, with combined position value rising to $124.80 billion from $107.48 billion, according to Insider Monkey's database. Microsoft, a fellow trillion-dollar technology company that has also recently emphasized premium, high-margin product positioning, saw holders slip to 273 from 282 even as position value grew to $66.51 billion from $63.58 billion.
John Ternus begins his tenure with strong hardware credentials and one of Apple's most consequential product launches in years. The iPhone Duo, higher-priced Pro models and Apple's growing emphasis on on-device AI give him several ways to reinforce Apple's premium ecosystem while selective price increases help offset rising component costs. Meanwhile, Apple now asks consumers to absorb higher prices while the firm still faces supply constraints and pressure to prove that its AI strategy can match its hardware leadership. Investors should watch whether Ternus can turn his product-development experience into sustained iPhone demand, stronger AI use and healthy margins without pricing too many customers out of Apple's newest devices.

Apple’s long-awaited smart home hub, which we’ve been referring to as the HomePad , is set to launch on October 13, according to Bloomberg .
The device is said to feature a 6-inch display and a design inspired by the iMac G4, and will launch alongside a HomePod mini update with new colors and a new Apple TV 4K with Siri AI support …
A previous report from the same source had said only that it was expected to launch “as soon as October,” but the latest report specifies October 13th.
Apple Inc. plans to make its long-delayed push into the smart-home market on Oct. 13, marking a critical product expansion for the company under new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus.
The iMac G4 was one of the company’s most iconic designs, with a hemispherical base and a free-floating screen that could be rotated, raised, lowered, and tilted to position it anywhere you wanted. I said a year ago that I very much hoped Apple would bring back this beautiful design for the upcoming product.
It’s previously been reported that the device will come in two versions: the tabletop one referenced here, and a second version intended to be mounted on a wall.
This one is going to be tricky for me…
I’ve waiting for this product for quite a while now, but over that time I’ve gotten into the habit of using HomePods and the Home app for controlling the house.  There will really have to be some standout features to make me shell out the $$.  Maybe they’ll surprise us and launch the rumored robotic arm version?
The upcoming device is expected to include a speaker to enable it to act as a HomePod as well as a smart home control panel. It’s expected to have a new operating system combining elements of iOS, tvOS, and watchOS – and to center around Siri AI.
Daring Fireball separately suggested that iPhone Duo review models would be handed over to tech writers on October 13 or 14, and that as Apple likes to do this in-person for high-profile products it would make sense to combine this with an event for the new products.
Today’s report says that the device is codenamed J490. Do you expect to buy one? Please share your thoughts in the comments.
